title: Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget
summary: Size the state behind every generated token, understand safe prefix reuse, and design block allocation and admission policies that keep streaming latency predictable.
learningObjectives: Calculate KV memory from model geometry and live token counts.
Explain how prefill and decode stress different serving resources.
Design exact, isolated prefix reuse and block ownership.
Defend admission, eviction, and batching decisions using latency and memory evidence.

sections.title: One request creates two different workloads
paragraphs: A serving engine receives tokens, creates persistent attention state, and repeatedly extends that state until generation stops. During prefill, prompt positions are known together, so the engine can process many positions in parallel and populate keys and values for every relevant layer. Prefill also produces logits used to sample the first output token. During ordinary decode, each sequence supplies one newly selected token per iteration. The next selection depends on the preceding iteration, although different requests can advance together. [The PagedAttention paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.06180v1) describes this lifecycle.

The service therefore needs two latency contracts. Time to first token includes queueing, preprocessing, prompt work, and response delivery. Inter-token latency describes the gaps once streaming begins; end-to-end latency includes the entire output. A long prompt can cause a slow first token without implying slow subsequent decoding. Conversely, a promptly admitted short request can stream slowly when it competes with many long resident contexts. Diagnose these cases separately instead of reporting one average request duration.

The KV cache contains intermediate tensors, not final answers or a semantic search index. It avoids recomputing preceding keys and values, but full-context attention still reads preceding state. A hit on a prompt cache therefore saves prompt computation; it does not eliminate the work of producing a long answer. This distinction matters when a product team proposes caching as the universal solution to latency.

sections.title: Count resident tokens before counting requests
paragraphs: For a conventional decoder with equal key and value head dimensions and full-context caching in every layer, raw KV storage is the product below. L is layer count, B is active sequence count, T is cached tokens per sequence, Hkv is KV heads, D is elements per head, and s is bytes per element. The factor two accounts for keys and values. Use KV heads rather than query heads for grouped-query attention. For unequal sequence lengths, replace B times T with the sum of cached lengths.

This is a tensor accounting equation, not a complete device-memory estimate. Add weights, temporary activations, execution workspaces, graph buffers, communication buffers, allocator overhead, and safety margin. Quantized KV may require scales and metadata beyond its nominal element width. Sliding-window or hybrid layers require a layer-by-layer sum rather than assuming every layer retains every token. Similarly, distributed deployments need the actual local layout: dividing global KV bytes by GPU count is wrong when some heads or layers are replicated.

The distinction between sequences and HTTP requests is operationally useful. A request producing several independent continuations can create several growing sequences. Shared prompt blocks reduce physical occupancy, while divergent outputs require private state. Track both logical token demand and unique physical blocks; either number alone can mislead capacity planning. The [Transformers cache guide](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.50.0/kv_cache) documents how cache strategies change memory and execution tradeoffs.
sections.formula: KV bytes = 2 × L × B × T × Hkv × D × s; unequal lengths: 2 × L × Hkv × D × s × Σᵢ Tᵢ

sections.title: A worked memory budget with explicit assumptions
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical single-device configuration with 32 layers, eight KV heads, head dimension 128, and two-byte KV elements. Each resident token costs 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB. One sequence with 8,192 cached tokens therefore occupies exactly 1 GiB of raw KV. Sixteen such sequences require 16 GiB; thirty-two require 32 GiB. These are calculated quantities, not measurements or claims about a particular model's throughput.

Suppose an illustrative 80 GiB usable-memory budget assigns 20 GiB to weights, 8 GiB to non-KV execution allocations, and 4 GiB to safety margin. The remaining 48 GiB holds at most 393,216 token slots at the stated geometry before block and metadata effects. Forty-eight sequences of 8,192 tokens exactly consume that raw budget and leave no allowance for further growth inside the KV pool. Reserving 2,048 additional tokens per sequence raises each reservation to 1.25 GiB, reducing this simplified safe count to 38.

This example exposes why a maximum-concurrent-requests setting is insufficient. The same request count can represent radically different prompt lengths, output commitments, or branching factors. Use a token or block budget in addition to a sequence limit. Treat the 38-sequence result as a conservative planning example, then validate real allocation behavior and workspace peaks with the actual engine. Prefix sharing can improve observed capacity but should not silently become a guarantee that disappears on a cold start.

sections.title: Blocks separate logical history from physical placement
paragraphs: PagedAttention lets a sequence's logically ordered history occupy noncontiguous physical blocks. A block table resolves logical positions to storage. Fixed-size blocks allocated as needed avoid reserving each request's maximum context and eliminate external fragmentation within that uniform pool. Unused space remains in partial tail blocks; smaller blocks reduce this waste but increase mapping and management work. Paging changes storage access, not which historical tokens exact attention considers. These mechanisms come from the [PagedAttention design](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.06180v1).

For an original arithmetic example, take 16-token blocks and the 128 KiB per-token configuration above. A block represents 2 MiB across layers. A 33-token sequence needs three blocks: 6 MiB allocated versus 4.125 MiB of raw state. Its 15 empty slots consume 1.875 MiB. Many tiny sequences can therefore have a noticeable allocation tax even though long sequences waste little proportionally. Compare occupancy against allocated capacity when investigating an unexpectedly full pool.

Sharing introduces ownership requirements. Immutable prefix blocks may have references from several sequences. Finishing one sequence removes its references without invalidating another reader. A shared block that must be modified needs private storage through a supported copy-on-write path; alternatively, the engine can restrict reuse to completed blocks. Never equate a request finishing with all its physical blocks becoming immediately reclaimable. Inspect the engine's exact block lifecycle, as described in [TensorRT-LLM cache management](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/advanced/kv-cache-management.html).

sections.title: Prefix reuse is exact computation reuse
paragraphs: A reusable prefix requires the same effective model computation: model revision, adapters, token IDs, preceding context, positions, and relevant multimodal inputs. Similar wording is insufficient. Inserting a timestamp at the beginning can invalidate everything after it; appending variable content after a stable system prompt preserves an opportunity for reuse. A matching suffix after a changed earlier token is not generally reusable because its hidden state depends on that earlier context. Tokenize and render chat templates consistently before lookup.

vLLM's [prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/) keys blocks using preceding-block identity, exact block tokens, and extra identifiers such as adapters or multimodal hashes. Its documented approach caches full blocks, so a matching partial tail does not imply an equal number of skipped prompt tokens. A model rollout should use a separate cache namespace or invalidate incompatible state. Treat a hit as a proof of computational compatibility, not merely a string comparison.

Reuse also crosses a privacy boundary. A tenant can potentially infer another tenant's cached prefix by measuring response timing for guesses. The [vLLM security guidance](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security/) describes secret cache salts scoped to a trusted sharing group. Enforce that scope server-side from authenticated identity; do not let clients choose another tenant's isolation value. Use robust identity hashing, bound metadata sizes, and avoid logging sensitive token content. Isolation intentionally reduces sharing opportunities, so evaluate capacity with the intended tenant boundaries enabled.

sections.title: Admission and eviction solve different problems
paragraphs: Admission decides whether a request can start without undermining active work. Check maximum context, requested output allowance, active sequence limits, and free or reclaimable blocks. Reserving every possible output token is conservative but can underutilize memory. Incremental allocation admits more work but requires a defined response when growth exceeds capacity: pause and recompute, offload, or reject additional arrivals. The policy must be explicit before an overload incident, including cancellation and cleanup behavior.

Eviction selects reusable inactive state to discard. Unreferenced blocks can be reclaimed while active referenced blocks require a coordinated preemption protocol. Removing historical tokens from an actively decoding full-attention sequence without reconstruction changes the computation; this is not ordinary cache eviction. [TensorRT-LLM's reuse documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/advanced/kv-cache-reuse.html) describes retention priorities and host offloading. Offloading trades capacity for transfers, so compare transfer delay with recomputation cost and expected future reuse.

A useful engineering objective is saved future prefill work per occupied byte, constrained by fairness and latency. Least-recently-used eviction is a reasonable baseline, but a scan of one-off large prompts can displace frequently reused prefixes. Consider tenant quotas, retention limits, and a minimum-reuse threshold. Maintain growth headroom for active streams, and apply backpressure before exhaustion causes repeated preemption. A high cache-hit rate is not a success if the retained cache prevents useful requests from entering the engine.

diagram.title: Three responses to memory pressure
diagram.caption: Select actions by state ownership and latency cost, not by a single occupancy threshold.

nodes.label: Reclaim inactive
nodes.detail: Discard reusable blocks with no active readers; later requests may prefill again.

nodes.label: Preempt active
nodes.detail: Pause a sequence with explicit offload or recomputation; streaming latency suffers.

nodes.label: Limit arrivals
nodes.detail: Queue with a deadline or reject excess demand while existing streams advance.

sections.title: Continuous batching spends the memory budget
paragraphs: Continuous batching updates the active set at iteration boundaries: completed sequences leave and admitted sequences join. [Orca](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu) formalized iteration-level scheduling. This avoids holding an entire fixed batch until its longest request finishes. Its effectiveness depends on having memory for newly admitted work, so allocation efficiency and scheduling are coupled. More available token slots can support a larger useful batch, but that does not automatically satisfy each stream's latency target.

Decode often has low arithmetic intensity, especially at small batches: weights and prior KV must move through the memory hierarchy for relatively little new-token computation. Batching amortizes weight reads across sequences, while each distinct long context still adds KV traffic. Eventually more concurrency can increase iteration time enough to harm inter-token latency. Prefill tends to offer larger matrix operations, but neither phase has a universal bottleneck independent of hardware, lengths, kernels, or batch size.

Bound the prompt work injected into each scheduling iteration. Chunked prefill splits a long prompt into smaller units so active decodes can continue between chunks; [TGI's overview](https://huggingface.co/docs/text-generation-inference/conceptual/chunking) explains this approach. Tune using realistic arrival patterns, prompt lengths, and output lengths. Record first-token and inter-token percentiles, queue age, preemption count, useful tokens per second, cache-hit tokens, and physical block occupancy. Run both warm-cache and cold-cache traffic: a popular shared prefix should improve performance, not conceal an admission policy that collapses when prompts change.

interview.question: A server using the hypothetical 32-layer configuration has 48 GiB available for KV. It accepts 48 requests with 8,192-token prompts and promises 2,048 output tokens each. Streaming later stalls and requests are repeatedly preempted. Diagnose the mistake and propose a defensible policy.
interview.answer: Each prompt consumes 1 GiB of raw KV, so the prompts alone exhaust the pool. Each full prompt-plus-output commitment requires about 1.25 GiB before overhead. A conservative raw bound is floor(48 / 1.25) = 38 sequences, with a lower operational limit after measuring block and runtime effects. Use block-aware admission, output limits, and active-stream growth headroom; reclaim unreferenced prefixes before preempting streams. Incremental admission is acceptable only with an explicit preemption and latency policy. Then test cold and warm workloads and inspect queueing separately from decode iteration time. Prefix sharing may improve utilization but cannot justify a worst-case guarantee unless that sharing itself is guaranteed.
followUps: How would four continuations per request alter logical and physical demand?

What evidence would make you reduce batch size despite available memory?

pitfalls: Sizing concurrency from model weight memory while ignoring growing KV state.
Using query-head count in a grouped-query KV calculation.
Assuming paging reduces full-context attention's logical context length.
Sharing caches on text similarity or token suffixes without preceding-context identity.
Treating unreferenced reusable state and active required state as equally evictable.
Reporting only warm-cache throughput while hiding cold-start latency and preemption.
checklist: Record layers, KV heads, head dimensions, cache dtype, and any windowed layers.
Calculate bytes per resident token and measure total non-KV allocations.
Set context, output, sequence, and physical-block admission limits.
Reserve active-stream growth headroom or document a measured preemption policy.
Version cache identity and enforce authenticated tenant isolation.
Verify reference release on completion, cancellation, timeout, and worker failure.
Benchmark cold and warm mixed-length traffic against first-token and streaming latency targets.

flashcards.front: Why separate prefill and decode latency?
flashcards.back: Prefill processes known prompt positions and creates KV; decode advances sequential output. Queueing or prompt work can delay the first token while memory traffic or scheduling slows later tokens.

flashcards.front: What is the basic full-context KV byte formula?
flashcards.back: 2 × layers × sequences × cached tokens per sequence × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per element. Two counts keys and values; use a sum of lengths when sequences differ.

flashcards.front: Which head count determines grouped-query KV size?
flashcards.back: KV heads, because query heads can share keys and values. Counting query heads overestimates the stored cache.

flashcards.front: How much KV does the article's 8,192-token sequence need?
flashcards.back: 1 GiB: 32 layers, eight KV heads, dimension 128, and two-byte elements give 128 KiB per token, multiplied by 8,192.

flashcards.front: Why do 48 one-GiB prompts fail in a 48 GiB KV pool?
flashcards.back: They leave no capacity for generated-token state. A 2,048-token output allowance raises each raw commitment to 1.25 GiB, giving a conservative bound of 38 before overhead.

flashcards.front: What does a KV block table accomplish?
flashcards.back: It maps logical token history to noncontiguous physical blocks, allowing incremental allocation without requiring one large contiguous reservation per sequence.

flashcards.front: Does paged KV eliminate every wasted byte?
flashcards.back: No. Uniform blocks avoid external fragmentation inside the pool, but incomplete tail blocks and metadata still occupy capacity.

flashcards.front: Why can a completed request leave its prefix blocks allocated?
flashcards.back: Another sequence may still reference them, or the engine may retain unreferenced blocks for later reuse. Completion alone does not determine reclaimability.

flashcards.front: Why cannot a matching suffix usually reuse cached KV?
flashcards.back: Its state depends on preceding context and positions. Changed earlier tokens invalidate computational identity even when the suffix token IDs match.

flashcards.front: What risk does a shared prefix cache introduce across tenants?
flashcards.back: Latency differences can reveal whether guessed prefixes were cached. Authenticated cache namespaces or secret trust-group salts restrict this timing signal's sharing boundary.

flashcards.front: How does inactive-cache eviction differ from active preemption?
flashcards.back: Inactive blocks have no current readers and can be discarded. Active state requires coordinated suspension plus offload or reconstruction; silently dropping history changes full attention.

flashcards.front: Why can increasing decode batch size eventually hurt streaming?
flashcards.back: Batching amortizes weight traffic, but more sequences and long contexts add KV traffic and computation. Longer iterations can violate inter-token latency targets.
Smaller prompt-work units let the scheduler interleave decode work, reducing long interruptions to existing streams at a possible cost to prompt-processing efficiency.

flashcards.front: Why is cache-hit rate insufficient to evaluate a serving policy?
flashcards.back: Retained prefixes can consume space needed by active work. Judge saved prefill work together with queueing, physical occupancy, preemption, throughput, and latency percentiles.
